name: Nano zinc oxide
lead: Nano zinc oxide refers to zinc oxide particles in the nanometre size range, used in sunscreens and other personal-care products as a mineral UV filter. For appearance, its practical benefit is cosmetic acceptability of mineral sun protection: Wikipedia notes that nanoparticles do not scatter visible light and so look transparent on skin, and Grokipedia states that the small size permits higher loadings without the white cast of larger particles, with particles often silica-coated to limit reactivity.[1][6] People who want daily broad-spectrum protection against sun-driven wrinkles, spots and tone changes without a chalky finish are the main audience.

The question researchers and regulators focus on is whether nanoparticles enter the body through skin. A 2019 volunteer study in the Journal of Investigative Dermatology was titled as showing lack of skin penetration or cellular toxicity after repeated sunscreen application, and Grokipedia reports negligible dermal penetration in human studies, with particles remaining in the stratum corneum, though some in vitro models suggest minor translocation under extreme conditions.[12][1] Wikipedia's zinc oxide article likewise states that nanoparticles are not absorbed more than regular-sized particles.[6]

In the EU, cosmetic ingredients in nano form must be labelled 'nano' under Regulation 1223/2009, and sunscreen use is assessed by the SCCS; US rules do not require nanoparticle labelling.[1][2] Laboratory studies document antibacterial activity and toxicity to aquatic organisms and cells in culture.[3][4][5]

paras: Nano zinc oxide gives broad UVA and UVB protection, by reflecting and scattering light according to Grokipedia, with a sheerer finish than larger particles.[1] Wikipedia describes zinc oxide as covering both UVA and UVB, as completely photostable, and as FDA-approved for sunscreen use, and says it is generally considered nonirritating and non-comedogenic.[6] Many sunscreens use nanoparticles, often together with titanium dioxide, because the particles do not scatter visible light.[6]
Other personal-care uses include anti-dandruff products.[1] Research uses include wound dressings, textiles and dental materials.[7][8]

Grokipedia reports negligible penetration in human studies and says the EU SCCS endorsed coated zinc oxide nanoparticles up to 25% for non-sunscreen dermal uses in 2016, conditional on low photoreactivity and particle size distribution under 100 nm.[1] A related wiki page notes that FDA classifies zinc oxide as GRASE for sunscreen without nano-specific restrictions.[2] A 2008 paper in the Journal of Biomedical Optics examined imaging of zinc oxide nanoparticle penetration in human skin in vitro and in vivo.[13] Wikipedia notes that some zinc from zinc oxide is slightly absorbed through skin, while nanoparticles stay in the outermost layer.[6]

Laboratory studies show cytotoxicity from reactive oxygen species and dissolved zinc in cell culture, and iron doping has been explored to make the particles less toxic.[4][5] Marine organism studies report toxicity that depends on aggregate size and ion solubility; one found nano zinc oxide formed larger aggregates in seawater than bulk zinc oxide while dissolving more.[9] Dissolution in different matrices has also been measured.[10]

Labels in the EU distinguish nano ingredients, while US products generally do not. Users who prefer non-nano mineral sunscreens often cite caution about particle size, while users who prefer nano formulas often cite the sheer, invisible finish that makes daily wear more practical on deeper skin tones.

A 2019 clinical study in volunteers examined repeated application of zinc oxide nanoparticle sunscreens and was reported as finding a lack of skin penetration or cellular toxicity.[12] A 2025 systematic review of topical zinc oxide nanoparticle formulations for acne identified eight investigations (five in vitro, two animal, one exploratory human) and discussed gaps before randomised trials.[14] Randomized trials of zinc oxide nanoparticle-coated socks have been run for pitted keratolysis in field settings.[15][16]

No studies found of nano zinc oxide for appearance outcomes such as wrinkles or pigmentation. Registered trials using zinc oxide nanoparticles are dental, for example cavity disinfection (NCT03478150, n=30).[11] Laboratory and animal work on antibacterial and wound-dressing uses is a separate category.[3][7]

Nano versus non-nano mineral sunscreen is a recurring theme in skincare discussions: some users prefer non-nano labels out of caution about nanoparticles, while others prefer sheer nano formulas for lack of white cast. These are general sunscreen views rather than documented claims.

card.summary: Nanoparticle zinc oxide: the invisible-on-skin version of the mineral filter, with debate centred on penetration and aquatic toxicity.
card.note: EU requires a "nano" label; US does not.

quick.overview:
Nano zinc oxide is zinc oxide in nanometre-sized particles, used so mineral sunscreens look transparent instead of white.

Human studies summarised in reference works report particles staying in the outer skin layer. No studies of appearance outcomes were found.
quick.mechanism: It reflects, scatters and absorbs UVA and UVB light; particles are often coated, for example with silica, to limit reactivity.
quick.risks: Laboratory studies report cytotoxicity and aquatic toxicity linked to dissolved zinc and reactive oxygen species. The EU requires nano labelling; the US does not.
